papers.title: Can LLM-Simulated Respondents Pre-Test Survey Questions? Evidence From Preregistered Prospective Validation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be conditioned to simulate behavioral responses, including survey responses, but it remains unclear whether and how these simulations can support downstream research tasks. Here, we evaluate whether simulated respondents can support pre-testing new candidate survey questions before fielding them, operationalized as prioritizing candidate survey items. Specifically, we rank candidate questions by their mean responses, which can reveal ceiling or floor effects; their variance, which indicates whether responses contain meaningful variation; and differences between subpopulations, which indicate whether questions capture distinctions between relevant groups within a population. We introduce a preregistered, prospective evaluation that commits model predictions before target human responses exist, ruling out memorization of those responses by design. Using two waves of a local survey (2025: N = 1,271; 2026: N = 1,161), we built simulated respondents from 2025 participants and preregistered GPT-4.1 predictions for 22 questions introduced in 2026. Simulations accurately ranked questions by mean responses (Spearman \r{ho} = 0.71) and anticipated which questions distinguished city from county residents (\r{ho} = 0.88), Black from White residents (\r{ho} = 0.68), and employed from unemployed residents (\r{ho} = 0.57), suggesting simulations can help prioritize questions before fielding. More broadly, our prospective, preregistered design provides a general framework for evaluating AI simulations without contamination from memorized target outcomes.

papers.title: Explaining intersectional segregation in multi-attribute social networks
papers.abstract: Segregation in students' friendships shapes their access to information and opportunities, and schools can reduce it by setting the composition of their classes. Yet segregation is usually measured one attribute at a time, although attributes such as migration background and sex are often correlated, so a preference over one can create segregation on the other. A single-attribute reading then attributes this induced segregation to the wrong preference and cannot identify which part of it a school can remove. In a network model with preferences over two correlated attributes, we derive in closed form the Coleman index, a standard segregation measure, separating the segregation due to each preference from the segregation it induces on the other attribute. In friendship networks of school classes in four European countries, ignoring sex inflates the estimated preference over migration background, increasingly so as the two attributes are more correlated. The closed form also shows what class composition can achieve. When students have no preference over one attribute, the segregation induced on it can be removed, whereas segregation set by a homophilic preference over the other cannot be changed. When both preferences are active, splitting a school with equal-sized groups and independent attributes reduces segregation only if the preferences pull in opposite directions. Judging a split by the school-wide average can hide classes that become more segregated. In the data, the split derived from the closed form removes induced segregation, and splitting does not lower segregation where both preferences are homophilic, as predicted.

papers.title: "I Do Intend to Deliver": Will LLMs Run a Marketplace Advance-Fee Scam?
papers.abstract: Online fraud is traditionally limited by the cost of the human labor needed to talk to potential victims. We ask whether hosted large language models will now supply that labor. We prompted ten off-the-shelf models to play the seller in the "free item, just pay delivery" advance-fee scam common on buy-and-sell sites, using a plain system prompt with no jailbreak. Each model played 30 conversations against each of four buyer personas, from credulous to guarded, with the same model playing the buyer (1,200 conversations). We label each conversation by what happened to the buyer's money, and validate the labels against two human coders. 737 conversations (61%) ended with the buyer paying in advance. Eight of the ten models played in almost every conversation, and running both sides cost about 2.5 cents per payment. Only the guarded buyer, who wanted a findable identity, resisted, and the most willing sellers got past it by inventing names and phone numbers. Sellers that recognized the scam still took the money in 133 conversations, usually reasoning about their own honesty rather than the buyer's risk. Several models protected the buyer without refusing, by conceding payment on delivery, so refusal rates alone misstate safety. We release the benchmark, prompts, code and labels.

papers.title: Differential Privacy for Network Connectedness Indices
papers.abstract: Researchers increasingly use data on social and economic networks to study a range of social science questions, but releasing statistics derived from networks can raise significant privacy concerns. We show how to release network connectedness indices that quantify assortative mixing across node attributes under edge-adjacent differential privacy. Directly adding noise to connectedness indices based on global sensitivity can result in poor accuracy both because connectedness indices have high global sensitivity and because a single node's attribute can potentially be an input to connectedness in thousands of cells, leading to poor composition. Our method, which is straightforward to apply, first randomizes node attributes, then analytically debiases downstream statistics, and finally adds noise to protect the presence or absence of individual edges. We prove consistency and asymptotic normality of our estimators for both discrete and continuous labels and show our method works well in simulations and on real networks with as few as 200 nodes collected by social scientists.

papers.title: Preserving Orientation and Transition Order in Transition Network Analysis: A Directed Topological Proof of Concept
papers.abstract: Transition Network Analysis (TNA; tna, Nestimate) models learning as directed Markov transitions. While Nestimate also offers sequence-level higher-order models, clique-based topological tools lose directional structure: tna::cliques() returns unordered mutual subsets without homology or convergence-divergence asymmetry, and undirected persistent homology in Nestimate symmetrizes transitions into clique complexes, erasing edge orientation and triangle order. We evaluate four directed constructions on group_regulation (9 states): Dowker sink/source complexes, directed flag complexes ($dFl$), and regular GLMY path homology, compared against row-permutation and degree-preserving null models ($B = 20,000$). Across $\tau \in [0.20, 0.28]$, $\beta_1^{dFl}$ exceeds the max-symmetrized clique complex $\beta_1^{\mathrm{sym}}$ by $1$; on $\tau \in (0.239087, 0.290401]$ (e.g., $\tau = 0.26$), $\beta_1^{\mathrm{sym}} = 0$ whereas $\beta_1^{dFl} = 1$, capturing the reciprocal consensus $\leftrightarrow$ plan loop (weights $0.3958, 0.2904$). On $\tau \in (0.146825, 0.172081]$, $dFl$ also leaves the directed 3-cycle {consensus, coregulate, emotion} unfilled. Regular GLMY path homology gives $\beta_1^{\mathrm{path}} = 0$ across all thresholds (lower-tail $p = 0.012$ for its sum over $[0.14, 0.30]$ under row permutation, reflecting in-degree concentration). Dowker analysis reveals significant sink-source asymmetry: 20-21 sink vs. 0 source 2-simplices across $[0.20, 0.28]$ ($p = 0.002$ at $\tau = 0.26$), driven by six behaviors converging onto consensus ($\mathrm{InStrength} = 2.667$). Thus, directed complexes unify feedback and sink convergence over one directed graph.

papers.title: Quantum Community Detection for Data Analysis
papers.abstract: Community detection offers an alternative to conventional methods for data analysis tasks such as feature selection and clustering, and detecting communities with quantum algorithms is a promising avenue for quantum speedup. We investigate quantum spectral community detectors, such as the modularity-matrix algorithm deteQt, in pipelines for both tasks. We first generalise deteQt to multiple communities by recursive bisection, and show that it recovers planted communities, and hence redundant features, in synthetic and small datasets. We then propose projeQt, which applies a spectral filter to the encoded modularity matrix through the quantum singular value transformation, retaining higher-order eigenvectors that deteQt does not use. projeQt acts on the generalised modularity matrix and extracts several communities at once, without recursion, by k-means clustering of a Gram matrix built from quantum state overlaps. On MNIST we demonstrate both pipelines, selecting informative pixels and classifying images directly by clustering, and find them competitive with standard community detectors.

papers.title: Copy, Predict, Code the Rest: Lossless Graph Compression with Decoder-Side Neighbor Prediction
papers.abstract: We present a lossless compressor for directed graphs. It copies neighbors from an earlier row, predicts further targets from the part of the graph already decoded, and codes what remains. Its main coder, the candidate-bit coder (CB), proposes a bounded set of candidate targets, mixes their probabilities adaptively, and codes the leftover targets with a popularity-aware model. The encoder tries a fixed set of vertex orders and storage directions and keeps the smallest file that decodes exactly. On the benchmark graphs outside our development set, the selected files are smaller than the best recorded WebGraph and Zuckerli files and the best published HyperFast results. These savings have a cost. CB decodes much more slowly than the baselines and supports only sequential access. A faster companion coder, CG, is still slower than the baselines on large graphs. An indexed variant, CS-RA, gives smaller seekable files than the measured access baselines on nearly all tested graphs, but its cold queries are slow, and it fails on one development graph. We also explain what successful and failed predictions cost, and when copying a repeated row saves information.

papers.title: Graph neural networks and the energetic cavity method for combinatorial optimization
papers.abstract: We study the use of graph neural networks (GNNs) for finding approximate ground states of Ising models. Efficiently finding these ground states is of broad significance because many combinatorial optimization problems can be formulated as an Ising model with the appropriate choice of couplings and fields. Exactly solving these problems is hard but there are many good heuristic methods. A lineage of these heuristics build from mean-field approximations: one approach uses the leading eigenvector of an appropriately defined matrix, another is the min-sum algorithm, also known as the energetic cavity method. Without modification, GNNs perform worse than both of these methods. We consider small modifications to the GNN to incorporate these heuristics and find that this considerably improves performance. While the modified approach is much stronger than other deep learning approaches, we still find that simulated annealing is generally as good for the same computational cost.

papers.title: Multi-Scale Temporal Structure of the Conti Ransomware Communication Network
papers.abstract: Communication networks provide a means of inferring broader organisational structure from accumulated local interactions. Cybercriminal organisations are particularly vulnerable to such inference, despite their secretive nature, because their distributed operation necessitates coordination through centralised digital communication infrastructure. The public leak of the Conti ransomware organisation's internal communications provides a rare longitudinal record of this coordination. Yet common approaches to analysing such longitudinal records aggregate interactions into a static network or model the communication process as stationary, both assuming a temporal homogeneity rarely tested for criminal organisations. Here we show substantial temporal heterogeneity at each scale examined in the Conti record, and demonstrate that much of it can be accounted for through appropriate, diagnostically guided choices of event representation and observation period. Collapsing rapid message bursts into conversational episodes brings communication timing closer to a constant-intensity reference and clarifies longer-timescale structure, which resolves into a sequence of distinct communication regimes, including a major transition following a coordinated platform migration. Even so, within these regimes heterogeneity persists, most evident in churn among peripheral participants, while highly active actors remain consistently observable. Together, these findings motivate explicit consideration of multi-scale temporal dynamics in the analysis, modelling and longitudinal monitoring of cybercriminal networks.

papers.title: Cross-Order Information-Guided Estimation for Non-Uniform Hypergraphs
papers.abstract: Many real-world interactions involve groups of nodes rather than pairs. A non-uniform hypergraph records such interactions as hyperedges of different orders, where the order counts the nodes in a hyperedge. Full estimation evaluates every candidate hyperedge, whose number grows exponentially with the order, and classical remedies sacrifice higher-order information or aggravate computation. The orders are not isolated: the lower orders, cheap to compute and rich in information, reveal where higher-order hyperedges are likely to occur. We propose CINE (Cross-order Information-guided Negative-sampling Estimation) under a latent space model in which all orders share latent positions. Starting from order two, CINE climbs one order at a time. At each higher order, CINE keeps all present hyperedges, samples a small subset of negative examples guided by lower-order scores, and corrects for the known inclusion probabilities to preserve the target of full estimation. CINE thereby lets users choose the trade-off between computation time and estimation accuracy: the retained orders and the sampling budget set the time, and the retained information provably approaches full-data information as the sampling budget grows. In simulations, CINE approaches the accuracy of full estimation at a small fraction of its computation time, and larger teams in MADStat reveal research associations.

papers.title: Principled Detection of Coordinated Manipulation from Aggregate Distortion and Account Reuse
papers.abstract: Coordinated manipulation is collective: plausible accounts can jointly distort ratings, rankings, and engagement. Existing defenses primarily construct evidence from identities, graphs, content, or co-activity. We introduce an aggregate-first evidence layer that treats distortion of a context-level outcome distribution as the primary evidence object. The engine observes only a histogram, count, resolution, and reference distribution; identities are withheld until interval evidence is fixed. Because raw discrepancies have positive finite-sample expectation, we subtract a matched null expectation to obtain signed evidence and account for reference uncertainty. Participation logs then accumulate these fixed increments across accounts. We characterize matched-exposure divergence, bound self-influence, establish finite-horizon separation, and derive an exact linear reuse law for paired contexts. We evaluate the mechanism with controlled rotation experiments and paired counterfactual interventions on historical Amazon review streams. Historical reviews provide the behavioral background; synthetic identities provide known coalition membership, and exact clean twins provide counterfactual controls. In a fixed-attack sweep against historical non-donor comparison accounts, reassigning the same manipulated events across identities with increasing reuse raises account-score ROC-AUC from 0.500 to 0.797. With activity- and exposure-matched clean twins, frequency is at chance while counterfactual attribution achieves ROC-AUC 0.744. Under a mean-preserving shape intervention, Wasserstein-1 and Jensen-Shannon evidence achieve ROC-AUC 0.909 and 0.967, while frequency and mean-based attribution remain at chance. Aggregate evidence complements repeated co-activity, improving mixed-mechanism ROC-AUC from 0.750 to 0.874 with a simple untrained combination.

papers.title: S\'anchez, Feij\'oo, or Abascal? Speaker Attribution and Ideological Congruence in LLM Personas Reading Posts on X of the Leaders of the Three Main Parties of the 29N General Election in Spain
papers.abstract: Source cues are central to political communication, yet reception studies with large language model (LLM) personas as synthetic audiences have not tested whether personas respond to who speaks and not only to what is said. With Spain's general election of 29 November 2026 in mind, we run a speaker-attribution experiment using 1,075 anonymised X posts by the leaders of PSOE, PP and VOX on four topics (the economy and employment, household costs, immigration and corruption) and 791 distinct value-grounded, LLM-generated personas. Each post was assigned to 300 topic-selected persona profiles, 150 grounded in the Inglehart-Welzel cultural map and 150 in Moral Foundations Theory, under four conditions: no author, S\'anchez, Feij\'oo or Abascal, yielding 322,470 complete persona-post quartets. Naming any leader lowered support for identical text, with the penalty for Abascal nearly twice as large as those for S\'anchez and Feij\'oo. The penalty follows the persona's elicited left-right self-placement (ideological congruence): left personas spare S\'anchez and right personas spare Feij\'oo, although ideology was never in the message-evaluation prompt. Corruption posts were penalised under every name, whereas on other topics the ideologically closest leader generally produced little or no penalty. The leader order matches public opinion in 48 CIS barometers (2022-2026) in all three groups and the sign of all twelve differences, but fits barometers before the model's 2024 knowledge cutoff better than recent ones. Our findings demonstrate that LLM personas evaluate political speakers through systematic, value-congruent priors: however, while they replicate human candidate rank-orders across survey barometers, this alignment is ordinal rather than quantitative, highlighting their utility for controlled source-effect experiments though not as substitutes for empirical public opinion surveys.
